question: How many tonnes of pizza do people in Chicago eat on an average day in 2026?

target.what: Total mass of pizza consumed by people in Chicago (city of Chicago, all pizza types: thin, deep-dish, frozen, restaurant, takeout, homemade) on an average day in calendar year 2026, measured as pizza mass as sold/served (not flour-equivalent)
target.cadence: Single annual average-day figure; no official series exists
target.caveats: Ambiguous scope: 'people in Chicago' could mean residents only (~2.7M), residents plus daytime/commuter population, or all pizza eaten within city limits (including tourists). Working interpretation: pizza consumed by Chicago residents plus visitors/commuters present in the city, i.e. consumption oc

candidates.hypothesis: US per-capita pizza consumption (or pizza restaurant sales) multiplied by Chicago population and a Chicago-vs-national adjustment gives total pizza mass; Chicago's strong pizza culture may push per-capita above national average. Target = (US per-capita pizza mass/day) x (Chicago population) x (Chicago adjustment factor).
candidates.data_to_find: US per-capita pizza consumption in pounds/tons per year (USDA ERS or industry reports, pre-2026); US pizza restaurant sales and average price per pizza to convert dollars to mass; Chicago metro population estimates. Substitute: national pizza sales dollars / average price per pie / average pie weight.

assumptions.name: Chicago pizza-culture adjustment factor
assumptions.rationale: Chicago is widely recognized for strong pizza culture (deep-dish, tavern-style) and the 1986 survey (p121) showed Chicagoans eating pizza 34.8 times/year vs LA <20 (p122), suggesting above-average consumption. A 30% premium over the US average is a moderate central value; the range spans no premium to a large premium.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to scale US per-capita pizza consumption (p1) to Chicago residents.
assumptions.falsified_by: Evidence that Chicago per-capita pizza consumption is at or below the US average, or a direct Chicago consumption survey.

assumptions.name: Average pizza mass per pizza meal
assumptions.rationale: A typical pizza meal comprises 2–3 slices; national-chain slices are ~110 g (p12–p17) but Chicago-style slices are heavier (p9–p10). A central value of 450 g per meal reflects a mix of thin and deep-dish slices, with a wide range.
assumptions.applies_when: Used with pizza meals per person per year to convert to mass.
assumptions.falsified_by: Direct measurement of average pizza mass consumed per eating occasion in Chicago.

assumptions.name: Trend factor for pizza meals per capita, 1986 to 2026
assumptions.rationale: No direct time series of Chicago pizza meals per capita exists. US pizza consumption has been roughly stable to slightly growing; a factor of 1.0 with a wide range reflects uncertainty about whether the 1986 frequency (p121) has risen or fallen.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to adjust the 1986 Chicago pizza meals per capita (p121) to 2026.
assumptions.falsified_by: Evidence of a strong upward or downward trend in Chicago pizza meal frequency since 1986.

assumptions.name: Average pizza weight (kg) for restaurant-channel pies
assumptions.rationale: A 14-inch chain pizza weighs roughly 0.9–1.1 kg (8 slices × ~110–140 g); Chicago deep-dish pies are heavier. A central value of 1.0 kg with a range of 0.6–1.6 kg covers thin to deep-dish.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to convert pizzeria pie counts to mass.
assumptions.falsified_by: Direct measurement of average pizza weight sold in Chicago.

assumptions.name: Average pies sold per day per Chicago pizzeria
assumptions.rationale: SF Bay Area pizzerias in 2012 sold 110–300 pizzas/day (p35, p36, p41, p42), but those are high-volume destinations. Chicago has many smaller neighborhood pizzerias; a central value of 60 pies/day with a wide range reflects the mix.
assumptions.applies_when: Used with the Chicago pizzeria count (p24) to estimate restaurant-channel pizza mass.
assumptions.falsified_by: POS or survey data showing average Chicago pizzeria daily pie sales far outside this range.

assumptions.name: Share of Chicago pizza consumption from restaurants/takeout
assumptions.rationale: Most pizza is consumed via restaurants/takeout; frozen and homemade are smaller channels. A 70% share with a range of 50–85% is consistent with US food-away-from-home patterns.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to scale restaurant-channel mass to total pizza mass.
assumptions.falsified_by: Evidence that frozen/homemade pizza accounts for a much larger or smaller share in Chicago.

assumptions.name: Chicago frozen pizza retail sales per capita relative to US
assumptions.rationale: No Chicago-specific frozen pizza sales data; assume Chicago per-capita frozen pizza spending is similar to the US average, with a range.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to allocate US frozen pizza retail sales (p123) to Chicago.
assumptions.falsified_by: Chicago-area frozen pizza retail sales data showing a materially different per-capita level.

assumptions.name: Average retail price per kg of frozen pizza
assumptions.rationale: Frozen pizzas typically retail at $5–$10 for 0.5–1.0 kg, implying $5–$20/kg; a central value of $8/kg with a range reflects the mix of private label and premium brands.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to convert frozen pizza retail dollars to mass.
assumptions.falsified_by: Chicago-area average frozen pizza price per kg outside this range.

assessment.note: Both are per-capita pizza consumption figures from the same Tasting Table page (same underlying compilation, likely Washington Post data); they are not independent of each other. p1 (US 23 lb/person/yr) is the usable anchor for a national per-capita route; p4 (Italy 17 lb) is context only and not transferable to Chicago.

All from one Frato's page (2012) citing USDA FoodData Central for chain slices. They consistently establish that a typical national-chain 14-inch slice is ~3.8-4.1 oz (~108-117 g) and that a Chicago deep-dish slice is 3.6-4.5x heavier. These are slice-weight conversion factors, not consumption levels; they support the mass-per-serving assumption for Chicago-style vs thin pizza.

Same SiteCity directory snapshot; p28 is a sub-count within p24. The 875 count is a listing count (includes possibly closed/duplicated entries), so it is an upper-ish proxy for active pizzerias, not a verified establishment census.

San Francisco Bay Area pizzerias (2012) reporting 110-300 pizzas/day; Gioia's 1,500/week (~214/day) is consistent. These are high-volume urban full-service pizzerias, so they likely sit above the Chicago average per-store throughput; useful as an upper anchor for pies/day, not a direct substitute.
Sauce volumes per day from the same SF Eater piece; consistent with the pie counts (roughly 0.1-0.2 L sauce per pie). Useful only as a physical-flow cross-check, not a direct Chicago input.

US per-capita cheese series from one source; internally consistent (32.1 -> 38.1 -> 39.9 -> 39.5 lb). Cheese is a pizza ingredient but most cheese is not pizza cheese, so this is a weak upper-bound flow check, not a pizza-mass anchor.
USDA cheese production and mozzarella share; same USDA release. Supports a physical-flow upper bound only; mozzarella is also used outside pizza.

One Detroit-style recipe page; internally consistent (dough = flour x 1.675, cheese/sauce scaling with pan area). Gives a defensible per-pie mass for a thick pan pizza (~0.9-1.1 kg for 10x14), supporting the restaurant pie-weight assumption.

p76-p78 are one Foodeist index (283 Chicago restaurants, $14.70 average listed price, 4.3% share); p75 is a separate Domino's store count. The Foodeist count (283) conflicts in scope with the SiteCity listing count (875) - different definitions (indexed sample vs directory listings), not a true contradiction, but it shows the pizzeria-count input is uncertain by ~3x.

2006 Chicago Tribune chain volumes: Giordano's 6M pies/yr in 14 city locations (~1,170/day/store) and Lou Malnati's 350k/yr in 3 city locations (~320/day/store). These are very high-volume deep-dish chains, far above an average pizzeria; useful as an upper anchor and to show chain concentration, not as an average.

Both are Chicago city-limits population from the same 2006 article (2.70M exact Census vs ~3M rounded). p101 is the precise figure; p102 is redundant rounding. Population must be updated to 2026 (~2.6-2.7M) via an assumption factor.
Roots Handmade Pizza weekly ingredient use (2012). Dough 800 lb/wk plus cheese 1,100 lb/wk implies a large pie throughput; consistent with a busy Chicago pizzeria. Ingredient-flow cross-check only.

Giordano's Chicagoland annual ingredient use (2012): 3.24M lb cheese/yr, 227k gal sauce/yr. With a cheese share of pie mass this yields a chain-level pizza mass; useful as a physical-flow cross-check for the deep-dish chain segment.
Lou Malnati's 4.3M lb dough/yr (2012). Dough is ~55-60% of pie mass, so this implies a large chain pizza mass; consistent with p95/p96 volumes. Cross-check only.

p121, p183 and p230 are the same 1986 Chicago Tribune survey figure (34.8 pizza meals/person/yr) repeated three times - one underlying measurement, not three. It is the only direct Chicago-specific frequency anchor but is 40 years old and must be trend-adjusted.
Same 1986 survey, LA comparison (20 meals/yr). Context for Chicago being above average; not a Chicago input.

2013 GrubHub/KUNC piece: deep-dish is ~9% of Chicago orders, non-deep-dish 10x more popular, yet Giordano's/Lou Malnati's sell 3x more deep dish than thin. These are order-share vs sales-share measures and conflict in apparent direction; they indicate deep-dish pies are much heavier per order, supporting a higher average pie mass in Chicago than a thin-crust-only assumption.

PMQ/Datassential/Slice industry context (2025): ~75,000 US pizza restaurants, indie sales levels, cost pressures. Supports the pizzeria-count and per-store-sales assumptions at national scale; not Chicago-specific.

One Spanish-language page: ~3M pizzas/day in the US and ~75,000 pizzerias. p203's unit is mislabeled (75, not 75,000) and p202 is a rough industry claim; together they imply ~40 pizzas/day/store nationally, a useful low anchor for average pies/day.
Sunbelt/PMQ industry stats: 83% eat pizza monthly, indie avg sales $446,885/yr, chain $770,808/yr. Supports per-store revenue and frequency assumptions; older (2017-2019) and national.
JB Alberto's (Chicago) profile: 18 drivers, 3-mile radius, 24-inch 'Giant' pie. Context on Chicago pizzeria scale and large pie sizes; supports a high per-pie mass for jumbo pies but is one store.

One 2025 survey (Current Backyard): Chicago DMA 5.66 pizzas/month at $28.20 vs national 5 at $23.51; city dwellers spend 41% more than suburbanites. This is the most recent Chicago-specific frequency/price evidence and directly supports a Chicago-above-national adjustment and a per-pizza price for converting dollars to pies.

One Clever 2024 ranking: Chicago 5.1 pizza restaurants per 100k (below the 8.4 national average), large cheese pizza $27.66 (43% above typical city), pizza passion score 93 vs 72 average, 68% of Americans eat pizza weekly. The low restaurant density but high price/passion is a genuine tension: Chicago has fewer but higher-volume/higher-price pizzerias, so per-capita consumption can still be above average.

assumptions.name: Chicago pizza-culture adjustment factor relative to US average
assumptions.rationale: Chicago DMA orders 5.66 pizzas/month vs national 5 (p216/p217, ~1.13x) and Chicago's pizza passion score is 93 vs 72 (p242/p243, ~1.29x), but Chicago metro has fewer pizza restaurants per capita than the national average (p232 vs p233), so the net adjustment is modestly above 1.
assumptions.applies_when: Transferring a US per-capita pizza mass to Chicago residents.
assumptions.falsified_by: A Chicago-specific per-capita pizza mass survey showing Chicago at or below the national average.

assumptions.name: Average pizza mass per pizza meal (kg)
assumptions.rationale: A meal is typically 2-3 slices; chain slices are ~108-117 g (p18/p19), so 2-3 slices is ~0.22-0.35 kg for thin crust, while Chicago-area slices are 3.6-4.5x heavier (p20/p21), pulling the mixed-city average up to ~0.45 kg.
assumptions.applies_when: Converting pizza meals to pizza mass for Chicago.
assumptions.falsified_by: A Chicago serving-size survey showing average servings well below 0.25 kg or above 0.75 kg.

assumptions.name: Trend factor for pizza meals per capita, 1986 to 2026
assumptions.rationale: No direct Chicago time series exists; US pizza consumption has been roughly flat to modestly rising over 40 years, and the 1986 survey was a peak-culture snapshot. Centered at 1.0 with a wide range to reflect genuine uncertainty.
assumptions.applies_when: Adjusting the 1986 Chicago frequency survey to 2026.
assumptions.falsified_by: A modern Chicago pizza-frequency survey showing a large sustained change from 34.8 meals/yr.

assumptions.name: Average pizza weight (kg) for restaurant-channel pies
assumptions.rationale: A 14-inch thin pizza is ~0.7-0.9 kg; a 10x14 Detroit-style pie with 527 g dough plus 318 g cheese plus 249 g sauce is ~1.1 kg (p63/p64/p65); Chicago deep-dish pies are heavier still. 1.0 kg is a reasonable mixed-style average.
assumptions.applies_when: Converting restaurant pie counts to pizza mass in Chicago.
assumptions.falsified_by: A Chicago pizzeria audit showing average pie weight well outside 0.6-1.6 kg.

assumptions.name: Average pies sold per day per Chicago pizzeria
assumptions.rationale: National average is ~40 pizzas/day/store (3M/day over ~75,000 stores, p202/p192); busy SF pizzerias do 110-300/day (p35/p36/p41/p42); Chicago chains do far more (p91/p95). 60/day reflects a mix of small and busy Chicago pizzerias.
assumptions.applies_when: Converting the Chicago pizzeria count to daily pie output.
assumptions.falsified_by: A Chicago pizzeria throughput survey showing average pies/day well below 30 or above 120.

assumptions.name: Share of Chicago pizza consumption from restaurants/takeout
assumptions.rationale: Frozen pizza is a large retail category (p123) but restaurant/takeout dominates urban pizza eating; 0.7 is a central split with a wide range.
assumptions.applies_when: Grossing up restaurant-channel mass to total pizza mass.
assumptions.falsified_by: Chicago retail scanner data showing frozen/homemade share above 50%.

assumptions.name: Chicago frozen pizza retail sales per capita relative to US
assumptions.rationale: No Chicago-specific frozen pizza sales data; Chicago's strong restaurant pizza culture may suppress frozen share, but city dwellers spend more on pizza overall (p227). Centered at parity with a wide range.
assumptions.applies_when: Allocating US frozen pizza sales to Chicago by population.
assumptions.falsified_by: Chicago-area frozen pizza scanner data showing per-capita sales far from the national average.

assumptions.name: Average retail price per kg of frozen pizza
assumptions.rationale: A frozen pizza typically retails $5-10 for 0.5-1.0 kg, i.e. ~$7-12/kg; p215's $28.20 is restaurant pizza, not frozen. 8 USD/kg is a central retail value.
assumptions.applies_when: Converting frozen pizza dollar sales to mass.
assumptions.falsified_by: Chicago retail data showing frozen pizza price per kg well outside 5-12 USD.

assumptions.name: Chicago population change factor, 2006 to 2026
assumptions.rationale: Chicago's population has been roughly flat to slightly declining since 2006 (2.70M in 2006 Census, ~2.6-2.7M in the 2020s). A factor near 1 with a modest downward tilt.
assumptions.falsified_by: Census estimates showing Chicago population above 2.75M or below 2.5M in 2026.

assumptions.name: US population, 2026 (persons)
assumptions.rationale: US resident population in the mid-2020s is ~335-342M; used only as the denominator to allocate national frozen pizza dollars to Chicago by population share. Range covers Census-estimate uncertainty.
assumptions.applies_when: Allocating a national retail total to Chicago by population share.
assumptions.falsified_by: A Census estimate placing 2026 US population outside 330-350M.

assumptions.name: Homemade pizza mass per Chicago resident per day (kg)
assumptions.rationale: Homemade pizza is a small channel: home baking of pizza from scratch or kits is a minor share of pizza eating, roughly 1-3% of total pizza mass. At ~0.3-0.5 kg total pizza per person per day, 1-3% is ~0.003-0.015 kg/person/day; centered at 0.004 kg.
assumptions.applies_when: Supplying the homemade channel in the channel-sum method.
assumptions.falsified_by: Evidence that homemade pizza accounts for more than ~5% of Chicago pizza mass.

previous_assumptions.name: Chicago pizza-culture adjustment factor relative to US average
previous_assumptions.rationale: Chicago DMA orders 5.66 pizzas/month vs national 5 (p216/p217), ratio ~1.13; passion score 93 vs 72 (p242/p243); but restaurant density is below average (p232 vs p233), so the net adjustment is modestly above 1.
previous_assumptions.applies_when: Transferring a US per-capita pizza mass to Chicago residents.
previous_assumptions.falsified_by: A Chicago-specific per-capita pizza mass survey showing Chicago at or below the national average.

previous_assumptions.name: Average pizza mass per pizza meal (kg)
previous_assumptions.rationale: A meal is typically 2-3 slices; chain slices are ~108-117 g (p18/p19), so 2-3 slices is ~0.22-0.35 kg for thin crust, while Chicago deep-dish slices are 3.6-4.5x heavier (p20/p21), pulling the average up. 0.45 kg is a mid-range value for a mixed thin/deep-dish city.
previous_assumptions.applies_when: Converting pizza meals to pizza mass for Chicago.
previous_assumptions.falsified_by: A Chicago serving-size survey showing average servings well below 0.25 kg or above 0.75 kg.

previous_assumptions.name: Trend factor for pizza meals per capita, 1986 to 2026
previous_assumptions.rationale: No direct Chicago time series exists; US pizza consumption has been roughly flat to modestly rising over 40 years, and the 1986 survey was a peak-culture snapshot. A factor centered at 1.0 with wide range reflects genuine uncertainty.
previous_assumptions.applies_when: Adjusting the 1986 Chicago frequency survey to 2026.
previous_assumptions.falsified_by: A modern Chicago pizza-frequency survey showing a large sustained change from 34.8 meals/yr.

previous_assumptions.name: Average pizza weight (kg) for restaurant-channel pies

previous_assumptions.falsified_by: A Chicago pizzeria audit showing average pie weight well outside 0.6-1.6 kg.

previous_assumptions.name: Average pies sold per day per Chicago pizzeria

methods.label: m1

p1.role: US per-capita pizza consumption, pounds per person per year

a1.role: Chicago pizza-culture adjustment factor relative to US average

p101.role: Chicago residents in the city limits (2006 Census)

methods.rationale: National per-capita pizza mass times Chicago population times a Chicago-above-national adjustment. Shared dependency: p1 is a national average that may already include frozen and homemade pizza, so this route covers all channels. Failure mode: p1's definition (as-sold mass vs flour-equivalent) is not explicit; a1 is weakly evidenced.

methods.label: m2

params.formula: p121 * a3 * a2 * p101 * a9 / k_days_per_year

p121.role: Chicago per-capita pizza meals per year (1986 survey)

a3.role: trend factor for pizza meals per capita, 1986 to 2026

a2.role: average pizza mass per pizza meal (kg)

p101.role: Chicago residents in the city limits (2006 Census)

methods.rationale: Chicago-specific frequency survey (1986) trend-adjusted to 2026, times mass per meal, times population. Shared dependency: p121 is 40 years old and a single survey; a3 and a2 are the dominant uncertainties. Failure mode: the 1986 survey may reflect a peak pizza-culture moment and its 'meal' definition may differ from today's.

kept.name: Chicago pizza-culture adjustment factor relative to US average
kept.rationale: Chicago DMA orders 5.66 pizzas/month vs national 5 (p216/p217, ~1.13x) and Chicago's pizza passion score is 93 vs 72 (p242/p243, ~1.29x), but Chicago metro has fewer pizza restaurants per capita than the national average (p232 vs p233), so the net adjustment is modestly above 1.
kept.applies_when: Transferring a US per-capita pizza mass to Chicago residents.
kept.falsified_by: A Chicago-specific per-capita pizza mass survey showing Chicago at or below the national average.

kept.name: Average pizza mass per pizza meal (kg)
kept.rationale: A meal is typically 2-3 slices; chain slices are ~108-117 g (p18/p19), so 2-3 slices is ~0.22-0.35 kg for thin crust, while Chicago-area slices are 3.6-4.5x heavier (p20/p21), pulling the mixed-city average up to ~0.45 kg.
kept.applies_when: Converting pizza meals to pizza mass for Chicago.
kept.falsified_by: A Chicago serving-size survey showing average servings well below 0.25 kg or above 0.75 kg.

kept.name: Trend factor for pizza meals per capita, 1986 to 2026
kept.rationale: No direct Chicago time series exists; US pizza consumption has been roughly flat to modestly rising over 40 years, and the 1986 survey was a peak-culture snapshot. Centered at 1.0 with a wide range to reflect genuine uncertainty.
kept.applies_when: Adjusting the 1986 Chicago frequency survey to 2026.
kept.falsified_by: A modern Chicago pizza-frequency survey showing a large sustained change from 34.8 meals/yr.

kept.name: Average pizza weight (kg) for restaurant-channel pies
kept.rationale: A 14-inch thin pizza is ~0.7-0.9 kg; a 10x14 Detroit-style pie with 527 g dough plus 318 g cheese plus 249 g sauce is ~1.1 kg (p63/p64/p65); Chicago deep-dish pies are heavier still. 1.0 kg is a reasonable mixed-style average.
kept.applies_when: Converting restaurant pie counts to pizza mass in Chicago.
kept.falsified_by: A Chicago pizzeria audit showing average pie weight well outside 0.6-1.6 kg.

kept.name: Average pies sold per day per Chicago pizzeria
kept.rationale: National average is ~40 pizzas/day/store (3M/day over ~75,000 stores, p202/p192); busy SF pizzerias do 110-300/day (p35/p36/p41/p42); Chicago chains do far more (p91/p95). 60/day reflects a mix of small and busy Chicago pizzerias.
kept.applies_when: Converting the Chicago pizzeria count to daily pie output.
kept.falsified_by: A Chicago pizzeria throughput survey showing average pies/day well below 30 or above 120.

kept.name: Share of Chicago pizza consumption from restaurants/takeout
kept.rationale: Frozen pizza is a large retail category (p123) but restaurant/takeout dominates urban pizza eating; 0.7 is a central split with a wide range.
kept.applies_when: Grossing up restaurant-channel mass to total pizza mass.
kept.falsified_by: Chicago retail scanner data showing frozen/homemade share above 50%.

kept.name: Chicago frozen pizza retail sales per capita relative to US
kept.rationale: No Chicago-specific frozen pizza sales data; Chicago's strong restaurant pizza culture may suppress frozen share, but city dwellers spend more on pizza overall (p227). Centered at parity with a wide range.
kept.applies_when: Allocating US frozen pizza sales to Chicago by population.
kept.falsified_by: Chicago-area frozen pizza scanner data showing per-capita sales far from the national average.

kept.name: Average retail price per kg of frozen pizza
kept.rationale: A frozen pizza typically retails $5-10 for 0.5-1.0 kg, i.e. ~$7-12/kg; p215's $28.20 is restaurant pizza, not frozen. 8 USD/kg is a central retail value.
kept.applies_when: Converting frozen pizza dollar sales to mass.
kept.falsified_by: Chicago retail data showing frozen pizza price per kg well outside 5-12 USD.

kept.name: Chicago population change factor, 2006 to 2026
kept.rationale: Chicago's population has been roughly flat to slightly declining since 2006 (2.70M in 2006 Census, ~2.6-2.7M in the 2020s). A factor near 1 with a modest downward tilt.
kept.falsified_by: Census estimates showing Chicago population above 2.75M or below 2.5M in 2026.

kept.name: US population, 2026 (persons)
kept.rationale: US resident population in the mid-2020s is ~335-342M; used only as the denominator to allocate national frozen pizza dollars to Chicago by population share. Range covers Census-estimate uncertainty.
kept.applies_when: Allocating a national retail total to Chicago by population share.
kept.falsified_by: A Census estimate placing 2026 US population outside 330-350M.

kept.name: Homemade pizza mass per Chicago resident per day (kg)
kept.rationale: Homemade pizza is a small channel: home baking of pizza from scratch or kits is a minor share of pizza eating, roughly 1-3% of total pizza mass. At ~0.3-0.5 kg total pizza per person per day, 1-3% is ~0.003-0.015 kg/person/day; centered at 0.004 kg.
kept.applies_when: Supplying the homemade channel in the channel-sum method.
kept.falsified_by: Evidence that homemade pizza accounts for more than ~5% of Chicago pizza mass.

The best estimate for the total mass of pizza consumed by people in Chicago (residents plus visitors/commuters present in the city, all pizza types, as sold/served) on an average day in calendar year 2026 is 97.72 t/day (80% model-based interval 53.99 to 177 t/day).

Two routes were combined by geometric mean with equal weight per block: a national per-capita route (88.81 t/day, weight 50%) and a Chicago-specific frequency route (108 t/day, weight 50%). Observed inputs are US per-capita consumption (23 pounds per person per year), Chicago population (2,701,926 residents), and [n] Chicago pizza-meal frequency (34.8 pizza meals per person per year). The rest are analyst assumptions: a Chicago culture adjustment (1.15), mass per meal (0.45), a [n]-to-2026 trend factor (1), and a population change factor (0.97).

The biggest risk is that the [n] survey is old and may reflect a peak-culture snapshot, and that mass-per-meal and as-sold definitions are uncertain. A current Chicago-specific consumption survey with clear mass definitions would most improve the estimate.

Key assumptions (proposed by the analyst model, not observed; code samples each one between the bounds shown):
- a1 Chicago pizza-culture adjustment factor relative to US average: 1.15 dimensionless, range 0.8367 to 1.673 (range widened by code); used by m1. Overturned by: A Chicago-specific per-capita pizza mass survey showing Chicago at or below the national average.
- a2 Average pizza mass per pizza meal (kg): 0.45 kg per meal, range 0.25 to 0.75; used by m2. Overturned by: A Chicago serving-size survey showing average servings well below [n] kg or above [n] kg.
- a3 Trend factor for pizza meals per capita, [n] to 2026: 1 dimensionless, range 0.7 to 1.4; used by m2. Overturned by: A modern Chicago pizza-frequency survey showing a large sustained change from [n] meals/yr.
- a9 Chicago population change factor, [n] to 2026: 0.97 dimensionless, range 0.8664 to 1.083 (range widened by code); used by m1, m2. Overturned by: Census estimates showing Chicago population above [n]M or below [n]M in 2026.

Method details (computed by code):
- m1 formula_mc: p1 * a1 * p101 * a9; Monte Carlo P10 to P90 56.45 to 139; result unit lb/year converted to t/day; own 80% width x/÷1.57 (Monte Carlo of the formula inputs)
- m2 formula_mc: p121 * a3 * a2 * p101 * a9 / k_days_per_year; Monte Carlo P10 to P90 52.6 to 216; result unit kg/day converted to t/day; own 80% width x/÷2.03 (Monte Carlo of the formula inputs)
- Combination: 2 block(s), equal weight per block (methods whose inputs overlap by at least half form one block; backtest errors set widths, not weights): B1 = m1: 88.81 (width x/÷1.57, Monte Carlo of the formula inputs); B2 = m2: 108 (width x/÷2.03, Monte Carlo of the formula inputs). by_construction: Only URLs leave the searcher (code regex); extractor, judge and final prompts never contain search result titles, snippets or the searcher's text. This holds by construction and is not measured.
residual_risks: The searcher sees post-cutoff search results and chooses which URLs are fetched, so page selection can be conditioned on the answer; only the URLs leave the searcher, and in backtests every fetched page is a snapshot dated <= as_of.
Live pages are used only when as_of is today; in backtests every page is an archived snapshot dated <= as_of.
The leak sentinel only catches registered official values in common formats, not paraphrased or derived numbers.
The model's own training data (knowledge cutoff unpublished) can include history before as_of; it cannot include the target if the target was published after the model's release.
Wayback snapshots are captured by a third party; a snapshot date <= as_of proves the content existed by then.
Assumption values are proposed by the judge model from its own knowledge, which can include the target's history before as_of; code checks their form, not where the number came from.
